questions.question: What is the difference between var, let, and const in JavaScript?
questions.title: Var Let Const
questions.direct_answer: var: function-scoped, hoisted (undefined), redeclarable. let: block-scoped, not hoisted to usable, no redeclare. const: block-scoped, must initialize, binding immutable (contents can still change for objects).

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand var let const beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: var: function-scoped, hoisted (undefined), redeclarable. let: block-scoped, not hoisted to usable, no redeclare. const: block-scoped, must initialize, binding immutable (contents can still change for objects).

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    V[var: function-scoped] --> H[hoisted as undefined]
    L[let: block-scoped] --> TDZ[TDZ until declaration]
    C[const: block-scoped] --> I[must initialize + no reassign]
    V -->|loops| SHARED[ONE binding — closures see final]
    L -->|loops| FRESH[fresh per iteration — closures safe]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The temporal dead zone (TDZ), the mechanism under let/const: let and const declarations ARE hoisted (the engine knows about them) but they're placed in the TDZ between the scope's start and the declaration line — accessing them in the TDZ throws ReferenceError (not undefined like var). This is a deliberate design decision: silent-undefined (var's behavior) hides bugs; the TDZ makes them loud.

The scoping mechanics, precisely: var declarations attach to the function's variable environment (one per function); let/const attach to the block's lexical environment (one per block). A function with 3 if-blocks has 1 var-scope but 3+ let-scopes — the isolation let/const provide.

The for-loop capture difference (the follow-up that tests depth): var i in a for-loop is ONE binding — closures capture the SAME i (they all see the final value). let i creates a FRESH binding per iteration — closures capture their own i. The pre-let fix was the IIFE wrapper or passing i as a parameter; let made the problem vanish (verified: let-loop funcs return 0 1 2).

questions.question: What is the difference between primitive and reference values in JavaScript?
questions.title: Primitive Vs Reference Values
questions.direct_answer: Primitives (string, number, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, bigint) are stored BY VALUE — assignment copies the value. References (objects, arrays, functions) are stored BY REFERENCE — assignment copies the pointer, both variables point to the same data.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand primitive vs reference values beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Primitives (string, number, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, bigint) are stored BY VALUE — assignment copies the value. References (objects, arrays, functions) are stored BY REFERENCE — assignment copies the pointer, both variables point to the same data.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The core difference, verified:

```js
// Primitives — copies are independent
let a = 42;
let b = a;      // b gets a COPY of 42
b = 100;
console.log(a);  // 42 — a unchanged

// References — copies share the data
let obj1 = { name: "Al" };
let obj2 = obj1;  // obj2 gets a COPY of the POINTER
obj2.name = "Bo";
console.log(obj1.name);  // "Bo" — SAME object
```

The primitives (7): string, number, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, bigint — immutable values stored by value. Comparing primitives compares VALUES (42 === 42 is true).

The references: objects, arrays, functions — mutable containers stored by reference. Comparing references compares POINTERS ({} === {} is false — two different objects).

The practical consequences:
1. Assignment: primitives copy the value; references copy the pointer (both variables see the same object)
2. Function arguments: passing a primitive gives the function a copy; passing an object shares the original
3. Mutation: primitive operations create NEW values; object mutations change the shared data
4. Equality: primitives compare by value; objects by identity

The copy solution for objects: const copy = { ...obj } (shallow) or structuredClone(obj) (deep) — breaking the reference sharing when you need an independent copy.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[a = 42] -->|b = a| C[b = 42 — independent]
    O[obj1 = {x:1}] -->|obj2 = obj1| S[obj2 → SAME {x:1}]
    S --> M[obj2.x = 2] --> B[obj1.x is also 2]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The memory model, precisely: primitive values live directly in the variable's slot (the stack-allocated binding holds the value). Reference variables hold a pointer to a heap-allocated object — the variable's slot is the ADDRESS, the data lives elsewhere.

The 7 primitives and their typeof: string, number, boolean (the values), undefined (absence of assignment), symbol (unique identifiers), bigint (arbitrary precision) — plus null (intentional absence; its typeof returning 'object' is the famous historical bug, verified in our run).

The function-parameter behavior (the interview's practical test): passing a primitive to a function — the function modifies its own copy, caller's variable unaffected. Passing an object — the function receives the same pointer; mutations inside the function are visible to the caller (the source of most 'why did my data change?' bugs). The defense: pass a copy (shallow for flat objects) when the function must not mutate.

The equality trap, expanded: '5' == 5 (loose equality coerces — true); '5' === 5 (strict — false). For objects, both == and === compare identity — {a:1} == {a:1} is false. Deep equality needs a comparison function or JSON.stringify (with its own limitations: key order, undefined values).

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined in JavaScript?
questions.title: Null Vs Undefined
questions.direct_answer: undefined: the variable declared but not assigned (the engine's default). null: intentional absence (the developer's explicit 'no value'). null == undefined is true; null === undefined is false.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand null vs undefined beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: undefined: the variable declared but not assigned (the engine's default). null: intentional absence (the developer's explicit 'no value'). null == undefined is true; null === undefined is false.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The distinction, verified:

```js
let a;              // declared, not assigned
console.log(a);       // undefined — the ENGINE set this
console.log(typeof a); // "undefined"

let b = null;         // the DEVELOPER set this
console.log(typeof b); // "object" — the famous bug (null is NOT an object)

// The comparison
console.log(null == undefined);   // true (loose)
console.log(null === undefined); // false (different types)

// Function defaults: parameters without arguments are undefined
function f(x) { console.log(x) }  // undefined
f();

// null is used for: explicit 'no value' — clearing a variable,
// 'not found' returns, JSON's absence of undefined
```

The semantic difference: undefined = 'the engine couldn't find a value' (never assigned, function returned nothing, property doesn't exist). null = 'the developer chose no value' (deliberate absence).

The gotchas to name: typeof null === 'object' (the 1995 bug, kept for compatibility — null is a primitive); null == undefined is true (the ONE loose-equality cross-type match that isn't coercion); JSON.stringify drops undefined properties but keeps null.

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    D[declared, not assigned] → U[undefined — engine's default]
    A[assigned null] → N[null — developer's choice]
    M[missing argument] → U
    R[no return] → U
    P[missing property] → U
    E[explicit clear] → N
    J[JSON] →|undefined| DROP[key dropped]
    J →|null| KEEP[kept as null]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The historical bug: null's typeof returning 'object' — the original JS implementation stored type tags in the value's lower bits; null (all zeros) collided with the object tag. The fix was never shipped (breaking the web). The correct check: x === null.

The undefined sources (the comprehensive list): (1) declared but unassigned variables; (2) missing function arguments (the parameter exists, value is undefined); (3) functions with no return (return undefined); (4) accessing a property that doesn't exist; (5) array holes. null appears ONLY by explicit assignment — the engine never produces it.

The void operator and the undefined identity: void 0 is the guaranteed-undefined expression (undefined can be shadowed in non-strict code; void 0 always evaluates to the real undefined). The modern code never needs this — strict mode and ES modules made undefined safe.

The JSON asymmetry: JSON has no undefined — JSON.stringify({a: undefined}) drops the key; JSON.stringify({a: null}) keeps it as null. The API-design consequence: null for 'present but no value', the key's absence for 'not applicable' — the convention most REST APIs follow.

questions.question: What are the falsy values in JavaScript?
questions.title: Truthy Falsy Values
questions.direct_answer: Six primitives: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy — including '0', 'false', [], {}, and () => {}. The coercion rule for if/while/&&/||.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand truthy falsy values beyond memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Giving a definition without explaining a practical trade-off.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect the concept to a small production example and state its failure mode.

sections.title: Quick Revision
sections.content: Six primitives: false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy — including '0', 'false', [], {}, and () => {}. The coercion rule for if/while/&&/||.

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The complete falsy list, verified:

```js
// All falsy:
console.log(
  Boolean(false),   // false
  Boolean(0),       // false
  Boolean(-0),      // false
  Boolean(0n),      // false
  Boolean(''),      // false
  Boolean(null),    // false
  Boolean(undefined),// false
  Boolean(NaN)      // false
);

// The truthy surprises (the interview traps):
console.log(
  Boolean('0'),           // true — non-empty string
  Boolean('false'),       // true — non-empty string
  Boolean([]),            // true — empty array is truthy!
  Boolean({}),            // true — empty object is truthy!
  Boolean(() => {})       // true — any function is truthy
);
```

The rule: if, while, &&, ||, and the Boolean() constructor all coerce their operand with ToBoolean — the six primitive values above coerce to false; EVERYTHING else (including all objects and arrays) is true.

The traps that catch even experienced developers:
1. [] is truthy — an empty array in an if-statement is TRUE (checking for 'array has items' needs .length > 0)
2. {} is truthy — an empty object is TRUE (checking for 'object has keys' needs Object.keys(obj).length > 0)
3. '0' is truthy — a STRING zero is non-empty, hence true
4. 'false' is truthy — the string 'false' is not the boolean false

The explicit checks: if (arr.length > 0), if (Object.keys(obj).length > 0), if (value !== '') — never rely on coercion when the value could be an empty container.

The default-value idiom (the practical use): value || 'default' uses falsy for the fallback — which BREAKS for legitimate falsy values (0, ''). The modern fix: value ?? 'default' (nullish coalescing — only null/undefined trigger the default).

sections.title: Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    V[value] --> IF{if(v)}
    IF -->|f/false/0/''/null/undef/NaN| F[falsy → else branch]
    IF -->|anything else| T[truthy → if branch]
    S[0 or empty string] -->|\|\| default| WRONG[0 replaced by default — the bug]
    S -->|\?\? default| RIGHT[0 kept — only null/undef default]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The ToBoolean specification (the exact rule the engine follows): undefined → false; null → false; +0/-0/NaN → false; '' → false; false → false. All other values (objects, arrays, functions, non-empty strings, non-zero numbers, true) → true. That's the COMPLETE list — there are no others.

The historical oddity: document.all — the spec gives it 'falsy object' status (typeof undefined, Boolean false) purely for legacy feature-detection code. The only object that's falsy.

The ?? vs || distinction (the modern interview follow-up): || checks truthiness (any of the 6 falsy values triggers the default); ?? checks ONLY null and undefined. For a parameter where 0 or '' are valid: value ?? 'default' keeps 0; value || 'default' replaces 0 with the default. The ?? operator is almost always what API-default code wants — the || default was the pre-2020 idiom that silently broke on falsy-but-valid values.
